document.title: Limited Protest of American Municipal Power, Inc. to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s 02/23/2026 Compliance filing

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
) 
Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
LIMITED PROTEST OF 
AMERICAN MUNICIPAL POWER, INC. 
 
American Municipal Power, Inc. (“AMP”) hereby protests the February 23, 2026 
compliance filing by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) in the above-captioned docket,1 
in which PJM proposes revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to 
comply with directives in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or 
“FERC”) December 18, 2025 order in Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al.2 As discussed 
below, AMP’s protest is limited to one specific aspect of the PJM Filing: the proposed 
revised definition for Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation (“Non-Retail BTMG”).3  
I. 
BACKGROUND AND INTRODUCTION  
Under the existing PJM Tariff, load served by all Behind the Meter Generation 
(“BTMG”), and more particularly, Non-Retail BTMG is, subject to certain requirements 
and limitations, eligible to be netted from daily load under section 34.2 of the PJM Tariff 
for purposes of calculating charges for Network Integration Transmission Service and 
other PJM charges.4 In the December 18 Order, the Commission found PJM’s existing 
 
1  PJM, 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access Transmission 
Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et al., Docket No. ER26-1479-000 
(February 23, 2026) (“PJM Filing”). 
2  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“December 18 Order”).  
3  See PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 15-18; id. at Attachment B, p. 43. 
4  See, e.g., PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 4-6. PJM proposes to revise section 34.3 of the Tariff such 
that it will now be the operative provision specifying the eligibility of Non-Retail BTMG to net against 
Network Load. See id. at 16 & n.48.

2 
retail BTMG5 rules to be unjust and unreasonable, and directed PJM to revise the Tariff 
provisions addressing certain generating units that are classified as retail BTMG.6 The 
Commission made clear, however, that it was not directing PJM to make any changes to 
its rules for Non-Retail BTMG.7 
The PJM Filing, submitted pursuant to section 206 of the Federal Power Act 
(“FPA”),8 proposes a number of changes to the Tariff provisions addressing BTMG, 
including a retail BTMG materiality threshold of 50 MW, and a three-year transition period 
for existing retail BTMG.9 PJM also proposes new or revised Tariff definitions for Behind 
the Meter Generation, Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation, and Retail Behind The 
Meter Generation.10 In accordance with the Commission’s directions in the December 18 
Order, PJM indicates that it is not proposing any changes to the Tariff rules for Non-Retail 
BTMG.11 
AMP and AMP’s load-serving utility members own and operate generating units in 
the PJM region that qualify as Non-Retail BTMG. AMP therefore strongly supports the 
 
5  The December 18 Order notes that the Commission and others apply the label of “retail BTMG” to the 
class of BTMG that does not qualify as Non-Retail BTMG, December 18 Order at P 7, while PJM’s filing 
includes a new definition of “Retail Behind The Meter Generation,” e.g., PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter 
at 7; Attachment B, p. 89. 
6  Id. PP 179, 221-224. Specifically, the Commission directed PJM to “propose a new MW threshold for 
the amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network Customers may net by using BTMG.” 
Id. at P 221. Recognizing that customers may have relied on the existing BTMG rules, however, the 
Commission required PJM to maintain the current BTMG rules for customers that fall below the new 
MW threshold level. See id. at P 179. The Commission also adopted a transition process for “retail 
BTMG,” including a three-year transition period and grandfathering of certain parties with existing 
contracts. See id. 
7  See id. at P 222. The Commission found that, given the existing Tariff limitation on the amount of Non-
Retail BTMG that is eligible for netting, Non-Retail BTMG does not present the same resource adequacy 
and reliability concerns as BTMG. Id.; see also id. at P 179. 
8  See PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 1 (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824e). 
9  See id. at 11-15. 
10  See id. at 15-18. 
11  Id. at 7, 15-16.

3 
Commission’s decision to preserve the current rules for Non-Retail BTMG. Likewise, AMP 
endorses PJM’s efforts to preserve the status quo as to those rules.12   
As discussed below, however, and notwithstanding PJM’s stated intent to preserve 
its existing Non-Retail BTMG rules in conformance with the Commission’s instructions, 
the proposed revision to the definition of Non-Retail BTMG included in the PJM Filing 
could be construed as preventing generating units that are merely eligible for application 
of the Non-Retail BTMG rules from ever participating in PJM’s newly established Co-
Located Load configurations. This literal reading would preclude a broad swath of PJM 
generators from supporting Co-Located Load because the set of generators eligible for 
treatment as Non-Retail BTMG includes, without reservation, generators “used by 
municipal electric systems, electric cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to 
serve load.”13 
Such an outcome, which PJM has indicated is not what it intended, would be 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory. Further, revising the Non-Retail BTMG 
definition is unnecessary and outside the scope of the Commission’s compliance 
directives. Even if in-scope, the proposed revised definition is at best ambiguous, and 
could be read to unjustifiably exclude otherwise eligible generation resources from 
participating in Co-Located Load configurations. Accordingly, in setting a just, reasonable, 
and not unduly discriminatory or preferential replacement rate in this compliance 
proceeding, the Commission should direct PJM to either revise the Tariff using the 
 
12  See id. at 16 (explaining that PJM is “seeking to avoid any inadvertent changes to the substantive rules 
pertaining to Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation,” and the proposed Tariff changes are intended 
to “preserve[] the status quo” regarding the ability of Non-Retail BTMG to net against load).  
13 See PJM Filing, Attachment B, p. 43.

4 
approach suggested herein, or simply not revise the Tariff definition of Non-Retail BTMG, 
as discussed below. 
II. 
PROTEST 
A. 
PJM’s proposed definition of Non-Retail BTMG should be rejected 
because it is unnecessary and could exclude otherwise eligible 
generation facilities from Co-Located Load configurations. 
The PJM Filing proposes the following revised Tariff definition of Non-Retail BTMG 
(new language underlined): 
“Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation” shall mean Behind the 
Meter Generation that is used by municipal electric systems, electric 
cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to serve load. Any 
facility that qualifies as a Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation 
shall be excluded from Co-Located Load configurations.14 
As a threshold matter, there is no evident reason to modify the definition of Non-
Retail BTMG as proposed by PJM. The PJM transmittal letter is silent as to why the 
underlined language above has been added to the definition of Non-Retail BTMG, or why 
such language is needed to comply with the directives in the December 18 Order.15 
 
14  PJM Filing, Attachment B, p. 43. This definition continues to define Non-Retail BTMG with reference to 
the definition of BTMG, which PJM also proposes to clarify in the December 18 Order. PJM proposes 
the following revised definition for BTMG (new language underlined): 
“Behind The Meter Generation” shall mean either Retail Behind the Meter 
Generation or Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation and refers to a generation 
unit that delivers energy to load without using the Transmission System or any 
distribution facilities (unless the entity that owns or leases the distribution facilities 
has consented to such use of the distribution facilities and such consent has been 
demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Office of the Interconnection); provided, 
however, that Behind The Meter Generation does not include (i) at any time, any 
portion of such generating unit’s capacity that is designated as a Generation 
Capacity Resource or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource; or (ii) in an hour, any 
portion of the output of such generating unit that is sold to another entity for 
consumption at another electrical location or into the PJM Interchange Energy 
Market. 
PJM Filing, Attachment B, p. 80. 
15  PJM states that similar language in the definition of Retail BTMG “is intended to provide clarity and 
direction to project developers about what pathways are available to serve load that is co-located, and 
to avoid unexpected and unintended hybrid scenarios mixing BTMG and the new transmission service

5 
Indeed, the Commission was clear that that it was “not direct[ing] PJM to change its rules 
for non-retail BTMG.”16 Accordingly, the proposed revisions to the definition of Non-Retail 
BTMG should be rejected as outside the scope of the compliance filing.17  
Even if PJM’s proposed changes to the definition of Non-Retail BTMG are deemed 
to fall within the scope of its compliance obligations, the revisions are at least ambiguous 
and could produce a result inconsistent with PJM’s stated intent and the Commission’s 
directives. The problem with PJM’s proposed definition of Non-Retail BTMG arises 
principally from the use of the word “qualifies” in the newly added text. For practical 
purposes, generation capacity that is designated as Non-Retail BTMG for load netting 
purposes under revised section 34.3 of the Tariff and is actually utilizing such netting 
provisions and therefore “excluded from Co-Located Load configurations” in the event 
and to the extent that the generator output is netted against load, as PJM apparently 
intends to convey through the new definitional text, may not be denied access to relevant 
usable transmission service. But by triggering the exclusion from Co-Located Load 
configurations based on whether generation merely “qualifies” as Non-Retail BTMG 
(rather than focusing on whether it is actually engaged in netting and limiting the 
preclusion to the extent of that netting), the proposed definition sweeps too broadly. 
Currently, generation “qualifies” as Non-Retail BTMG under the Tariff if it: (1) 
meets the definition of BTMG; and (2) is “used by municipal electric systems, electric 
 
products the Commission has directed in the [December 18 Order].” PJM Filing, Transmittal Letter at 
18. As discussed herein, however, PJM’s proposed revised definition of Non-Retail BTMG would reduce 
the clarity of options available to generation owners and developers considering pathways to serve co-
located load under the Tariff. 
16  December 18 Order at P 222. 
17  See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 173 FERC ¶ 61,244, at P 50 (2020) (explaining that 
“[c]ompliance filings must be limited to the specific directives ordered by the Commission,” and directing 
PJM to remove certain proposed Tariff provisions included in a compliance filing).

6 
cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to serve load.”18 Thus, any generating 
unit that could arguably fall within these criteria might be said to “qualify” as Non-Retail 
BTMG, even if the unit is not used to offset load for purposes of charges assessed under 
the PJM Tariff. 
It is possible that owners of generation resources including municipal electric 
systems, electric cooperatives, or electric distribution companies (“EDCs”) with generator 
capacity that is not netted against load (i.e., are not serving in whole or in part as Non-
Retail BTMG) may seek to serve Co-Located Load, to the extent such resources are 
otherwise eligible to do so under the PJM Tariff. Significantly, Part VIII, Subpart E, section 
415 of the currently effective Tariff allows Non-Retail BTMG resources to be partially 
treated as Non-Retail BTMG and also to obtain Capacity Resource or Energy Resource 
status in PJM’s markets. Given that, there does not seem to be a valid rationale for 
excluding these resources from a Co-Located Load configuration. 
But to the extent that such resources might still be said to “qualify” as Non-Retail 
BTMG under the Tariff, these resources could be needlessly excluded from Co-Located 
Load arrangements under PJM’s proposed revisions to the Non-Retail BTMG definition. 
PJM identifies no rationale for excluding otherwise eligible non-netting generation owned 
by municipal electric systems, electric cooperatives, or EDCs from participation in Co-
Located Load configurations simply because they might be deemed to “qualify” as Non-
Retail BTMG. Such an (apparently unintentional) exclusion would frustrate the objective 
of making the three proposed new transmission service options available in these 
 
18  See PJM Filing, Attachment B, p. 43.

7 
circumstances to serve Co-Located Load, thereby restricting Co-Located Load from 
accessing service from this broad set of PJM generators. 
Finally, it is not clear that PJM’s proposed exclusionary language is needed in 
principle. To the extent that all or a portion of a municipal, cooperative, or EDC generator 
is engaged in netting under the existing Non-Retail BTMG Tariff provisions, the netted 
portion of its output necessarily will not need access to one of the three newly proposed 
types of transmission service. Furthermore, PJM has not explained on the record why it 
would be reasonable to prohibit, for example, a municipal generating unit from serving a 
portion of a Co-Located Load, while the balance of that load is served from other 
generating resources or market purchases that are supported by any of the three new 
types of transmission service. Absent PJM’s proposed modification of the Non-Retail 
BTMG definition, it seems that the balance of PJM’s proposal, coupled with existing Tariff 
provisions, would permit such a supply combination. Thus, without a rational explanation 
in the record, the Commission should reject PJM’s revisions to the Non-Retail BTMG 
definition as unduly discriminatory and inconsistent with the Commission’s directives in 
the December 18 Order. 
B. 
Alternatively, the Commission should direct PJM to revise its 
proposed definition of Non-Retail BTMG. 
If the Commission does not outright reject PJM’s revisions to the definition of Non-
Retail BTMG, AMP proposes the following revised definition in lieu of PJM’s proposal:  
“Non-Retail Behind The Meter Generation” shall mean Behind the 
Meter Generation that is used by municipal electric systems, electric 
cooperatives, or electric distribution companies to serve load. The 
output from any facility that (1) qualifies as Non-Retail Behind The 
Meter Generation, and (2) is used for netting pursuant to Tariff, Part 
III, 
section 
34.3 shall 
be 
excluded 
from 
Co-Located 
Load 
configurations, in the event of and to the extent of that netting.

8 
AMP’s alternative preserves PJM’s apparent intent that generating capacity designated 
as Non-Retail BTMG for netting purposes should not be eligible for Co-Located Load 
configurations, while making clear that the mere fact that a generator, as a conceptual 
matter, might qualify as Non-Retail BTMG does not render the generator wholly ineligible 
to participate in such configurations, to the extent it otherwise qualifies under the Tariff.  
 
Directing PJM to revise its proposal as described above is well within the 
Commission’s authority. PJM submitted its filing in this docket pursuant to FPA section 
206 for the purpose of establishing a just and reasonable replacement rate given the 
Commission’s finding that certain aspects of the existing PJM Tariff were unjust, 
unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential. The Commission has the 
obligation to fix the just and reasonable replacement rate,19 and it is not restricted to 
accepting or rejecting PJM’s compliance proposal submitted under FPA section 206.20 
 
 
 
19  See, e.g., 16 U.S.C. § 824e(a); Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 663 (D.C. Cir. 
2017) (citation modified) (“When the Commission changes an existing filed rate under section 206, it is 
the Commission’s burden to prove the reasonableness of its change in methodology.”). 
20  See, e.g., Bldg. for the Future Through Elec. Reg’l Transmission Planning and Cost Allocation, Order 
No. 1920-B, 191 FERC ¶ 61,026, at PP 46-51 (2025) (rejecting arguments that compliance filings in a 
FPA section 206 proceeding implicate public utilities’ FPA section 205 filing rights).

9 
III. 
CONCLUSION 
WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, American Municipal Power, Inc. 
respectfully requests that the Commission reject PJM’s proposal to revise the existing 
Tariff definition of Non-Retail BTMG as outside the scope of this compliance proceeding. 
Even if PJM’s proposed revisions to the Non-Retail BTMG definition are deemed to be 
within the scope of this proceeding, the Commission should direct PJM to revise the 
proposed definition of Non-Retail BTMG as described herein. 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
/s/ John McCaffrey
